assessment.nobel_worthiness: Their political-economy models of trade protection and their joint work on innovation, trade and endogenous growth reshaped how economists treat trade policy and long-run growth. The ideas are foundational and are now used routinely in teaching and policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: The Helpman-Grossman partnership is clear and the credit is concentrated in two people. The candidate's own framing emphasises trade policy and special-interest politics, but the growth-and-trade work is also joint, so the prize citation would need to be drawn carefully.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the late 1980s to the 1990s and has been confirmed over decades by theory, empirical tests and textbook adoption. Timing is not a concern.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would frame the prize around trade policy or around innovation-driven growth.
Possible overlap with the 2025 growth prize and with earlier trade prizes.
Helpman also appears in B030, which could split support.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural demand estimation with differentiated products and dynamic oligopoly models became the standard toolkit for merger review, antitrust analysis and applied industrial organisation. It is a methodological advance with large downstream use.
assessment.attribution: The core demand-estimation contribution is the BLP framework, credited to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. Pakes also has separate dynamic-games work, with Ericson and with Benkard. Bresnahan and Reiss made earlier foundational contributions that a three-person limit leaves out.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1990s and is confirmed by widespread use in academia, competition authorities and industry for three decades.
uncertainties: Selecting three names from a seven-name list involves difficult credit trade-offs.
Whether the committee sees the contribution as primarily methodological, and whether it ranks above other estimation-method prizes.
The relative weight of the Bresnahan and Reiss contributions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The China-shock research and the task-based view of technology changed how economists and policymakers understand trade, automation, local labour markets and wage inequality. It links causal empirical evidence to major policy debates and is close to current interest in technological change and displacement.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock papers are credited to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. Katz's earlier work on skill-biased change is related but separate, and the task framework involves others outside this list.
assessment.maturity: The core papers date from 2013 to 2016, and replication and extension are extensive. The long-run welfare conclusions are still debated.
uncertainties: Recent prizes have already rewarded work on technology, institutions and growth, so there may be some thematic overlap.
Debate over the persistence and magnitude of the trade effects.
Where the task-based framework should be credited, since it falls partly outside the listed names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work built a systematic economic theory and empirics of constitutions, electoral rules, state capacity and fiscal policy. It links institutions to policy outcomes and to development, drawing on historical as well as contemporary data. It is a coherent research programme with broad influence in political economy.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are jointly associated with the constitutions and electoral-rules programme. Besley and Persson are jointly associated with state capacity. All three can reasonably be credited as a group.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1990s to the 2010s and is thoroughly confirmed, with extensive follow-on research.
uncertainties: The 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity may reduce the appetite for a closely related topic.
Some credit is shared with others in political economy outside the list.
As the profile notes, a Lund-based historian may also be familiar with this literature, which is a possible disclosure rather than a merit factor.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The construction of long-run top-income and wealth series from tax records changed the empirical foundation of inequality research and the public debate. It is highly influential, and the long-run historical data approach is a major methodological contribution.
assessment.attribution: The long-run top-incomes work is credited to Piketty and Saez, and the offshore-wealth and distributional national accounts work to Zucman. Many collaborators, including Atkinson, contributed to the early series, so the list is not complete.
assessment.maturity: The top-incomes series date from the early 2000s and the broader wealth work from the 2010s. The data and basic findings are widely used, but some results on the trend in wealth concentration are still contested.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes about wealth-inequality measurement and about the interpretation of the r > g framework.
Atkinson's contribution cannot be rewarded because he has died, which complicates attribution.
The theoretical contribution is weaker than the empirical one.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, nominal rigidities and the associated monetary-policy rules form the theoretical core of modern central banking. The impact on policy practice is very large.
assessment.attribution: Attribution is the main problem. The framework was assembled by many contributors, including Calvo on pricing, Taylor on policy rules, Woodford, Gali and Gertler on the synthesis and Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets on estimation. Any three-person selection is arbitrary and leaves out significant contributors.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1980s to the 2000s and is thoroughly tested, though the 2008 and 2021-22 episodes raised questions about the framework.
uncertainties: Credit allocation is very contested among eight listed names.
Criticism of the framework after the financial crisis and the inflation surge.
Previous prizes already rewarded related macroeconomics and monetary policy work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation literature gave a quantifiable account of how distortions in the allocation of resources across firms lower aggregate productivity and explain cross-country income gaps. It connects micro data to macro development and is widely cited.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) is the key paper, and Restuccia and Rogerson's earlier work is closely related. Rogerson is not on the listed names, which complicates the credit.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from 2008 to 2009 and has proven influential, but the measurement of misallocation is still debated.
uncertainties: Measurement error and the interpretation of dispersion in marginal products.
Omission of Rogerson from the credited names.
Relationship to the 2025 growth prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data brought new measurement to the study of intergenerational mobility and neighbourhood effects. It combines new historical-style datasets with modern causal methods and has had a large influence on policy debate.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the central figure, with Hendren and Friedman as long-term collaborators. Katz's Moving to Opportunity work is also related but not proposed here. Credit among a very large collaborative team is hard to partition.
assessment.maturity: The core work dates from the 2010s, so it is recent. Some findings, including neighbourhood causal effects, are well supported, but the long-run consequences are still unfolding.
uncertainties: Relative recency compared with the older candidates.
Ongoing replication and interpretation questions about mobility estimates.
The large collaborative team makes a three-name attribution difficult.
